title: Ramayana Review: Critics Hail the Spectacle, Split on the Storytelling
excerpt: Bollywood Hungama gave Nitesh Tiwari's Hindi epic a perfect 5/5, but international critics who saw the English dub ranged from IGN's 4/10 to Screen Rant's 7/10 — praising the scale, score and Yash's Ravana while faulting the pacing and crowding.
body:
• Nitesh Tiwari's Hindi-language epic Ramayana — released internationally as Ramayana: Rise of a Legend — opens in theatres in India and the United States on Thursday, November 5, 2026, with Part 2 due at Diwali 2028, according to Bollywood Hungama.
  • Critics are split down the middle: Bollywood Hungama gave the film 5/5, while the scored international reviews ranged from IGN's 4/10 to Screen Rant's 7/10, with IndieWire awarding a grade of B.
  • Every critic read for this review praised the scale, the Hans Zimmer and A. R. Rahman score and Yash's Ravana; they divided over pacing, a crowded story and, in the English dub, visual effects and AI-assisted lip-sync.
  • US theatres will play the film in Hindi and English, according to Screen Rant — critics who saw the dub suggest Hindi is the safer seat.

The first reviews of Ramayana are in, and they do not agree — which is itself the story. Nitesh Tiwari's retelling of Valmiki's epic premiered in Los Angeles on October 27, and international reviews appeared after the embargo lifted on October 30, according to Zoom TV. The first major Indian review, by Taran Adarsh for Bollywood Hungama, arrived on October 31 with a perfect score. The international critics who saw the English-language version were cooler. Read together, the five named reviews describe the same film in two registers: a landmark spectacle at home, and an impressive but overstuffed epic abroad.

The film is a Hindi-language production, written by Tiwari and Shridhar Raghavan. Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama, Sai Pallavi plays Sita and Yash plays Ravana, with Ravi Dubey as Lakshmana and a much-discussed appearance by Sunny Deol that Bollywood Hungama pointedly refused to spoil. It is produced by Namit Malhotra's Prime Focus with the visual effects company DNEG and Yash's Monster Mind Creations. The score is by Hans Zimmer and A. R. Rahman — Zimmer's first Indian film, IndieWire noted — and A. R. Rahman also composed the songs.

"Read together, the five named reviews describe the same film in two registers: a landmark spectacle at home, and an impressive but overstuffed epic abroad."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=T0Uduwg2W2w

What the critics said

  • The consensus: Five named reviews were read. The four with a numeric score — Bollywood Hungama 5/5, Screen Rant 7/10, Next Best Picture 5/10, IGN 4/10 — average just over 3/5, with IndieWire's grade of B at the positive end. Critics agree on the craft — scale, score, Ravana — and part company on whether the storytelling underneath is watertight, as Bollywood Hungama found it, or too densely packed for the characters to breathe, as the other three argued.
  • What's praised: Scale first. Adarsh wrote that audiences have not witnessed anything as magnificent on the Indian screen, praising the Brahma–Ravana opening, the Sita Swayamvar and the emotional pre-interval stretch. Zachary called the film an impressive cinematic achievement on a purely visual and technical level, and Lago credited Tiwari with the operatic scale the story needs. The score drew praise across the split — terrific for Bollywood Hungama, bombastic in the right way for Lago, and singled out by Zilko, who noted the film will never bore viewers. Yash is the one point of unanimity: superb and imposing for Bollywood Hungama, magnetic for Next Best Picture, and, for Zachary, the character with the clear personality the rest of the cast needed more of. Kapoor drew praise for grace and quiet strength, and Sai Pallavi for dignity and warmth.
  • What's criticized: The international reviews converge on crowding. Zilko argued that when every scene plays like a climax, the audience never gets the quieter moments that would make each turning point matter. Zachary found Rama and Sita one-note — rooted so thoroughly in their mythological selves that they do not always feel fully human — and said a death late in the film does not land as it should. Lago faulted the pacing, said the visual effects often feel weightless, comparing stretches to cutscenes from an outdated video game, and criticised the English dub's generative-AI lip-sync as a distraction. IGN's Siddhant Adlakha, in the verdict quoted by Rotten Tomatoes, called it a majestic epic that falls victim to clunky action, eye-sore CGI and awkward AI lip-syncing. Bollywood Hungama raised none of these objections — a gap readers should weigh, because the two camps were not watching identical cuts.
  • What this means for you: Go for the spectacle, and choose your version deliberately. The film opens on Thursday, November 5 in India and the United States; Screen Rant reports US theatres will play it in both Hindi and English, Zoom TV reported an IMAX rollout is planned, and Bollywood Hungama's advice — the largest screen possible — is the one recommendation every review supports. Check the length before you book: the Hindi version was certified at 195 minutes, according to Adarsh's post as reported by News18, while the English cuts reviewed abroad were listed at 154 minutes by Screen Rant and 167 minutes by Next Best Picture. If the dub complaints matter to you, Lago's review suggests subtitles are a smaller price than the AI-adjusted dub. And know this is only Part 1: Bollywood Hungama says Part 2 arrives at Diwali 2028, so the ending is a midpoint, not a conclusion.

That split is a fair map of what diaspora audiences are likely to feel: readers who grew up with the epic will find the devotion Bollywood Hungama celebrated, and readers coming to it as a fantasy epic will hit the friction the international critics did.

image_caption: A still from Ramayana: Part 1 shows Rama standing before a waterfall. Critics praised the film's scale and spectacle while dividing on its storytelling.
nri_angle: The film opens in US theatres on November 5 in both Hindi and English, and the split between Indian and international critics maps directly onto the choice diaspora viewers face between the original Hindi cut and the English dub.
author: Diaspora Desk

critics.name: Taran Adarsh
critics.verdict: Ramayana is not merely a film; IT'S AN EXPERIENCE. It is a film that makes India proud.

critics.name: Christian Zilko
critics.verdict: Calling “Ramayana” epic may be a cliche, but there's really no other word that would suffice.

critics.name: Brandon Zachary
critics.verdict: On a purely visual and technical level, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is an impressive cinematic achievement.

critics.name: Giovanni Lago
critics.verdict: Audiences can still be swept up by “Ramayana,” even if it feels so stuffed at times that it might've needed a “Game of Thrones”-level television adaptation to flesh out its narrative fully.

critics.name: Siddhant Adlakha
critics.verdict: A majestic epic falls victim to clunky action, eye-sore CGI, and awkward AI lip-syncing in what is, unfortunately, just a Part 1.
